prompt: What makes a data mart dependent?

choices.text: It is built from the warehouse, with the warehouse's dimensions
choices.why: Right. It says nothing the warehouse does not say.

choices.text: It is stored as views
choices.why: Views are one form; summary tables built from the star are dependent too.

choices.text: Its team depends on IT to run it
choices.why: Who runs it is not the point; where it comes from is.

choices.text: It is loaded after the warehouse each night
choices.why: An independent mart can load at the same hour.

prompt: Why are independent marts the usual way companies start?

choices.text: They are cheaper to store than one warehouse
choices.why: Storage is not the reason; they duplicate it.

choices.text: They give the same answers as a warehouse, only faster, because each holds less data
choices.why: The same answers is exactly what they do not give.

choices.text: One team, one question, one load
choices.why: Right. Nobody has to own a warehouse first.

choices.text: Kimball's method requires them first
choices.why: Kimball's marts share dimensions, so they are dependent.

prompt: How much disk does Ana's `mart_sales.monthly` take?

choices.text: About one row per shop and month
choices.why: That is what a summary table would hold.

choices.text: None for rows: it stores a query
choices.why: Right. Every answer is computed from fact_sales when asked.

choices.text: As much as fact_sales, since it reads every row
choices.why: Reading is not storing.

choices.text: A copy of the three tables it joins
choices.why: A view copies nothing.

prompt: In December 2025, Online sold 347,127,604 centavos out of 755,814,482. What percentage is that, to one decimal place?
When views over a big fact table become slow, what keeps the mart dependent?

choices.text: A load of the mart from the extract, which is faster than the star
choices.why: Loaded from the extract, it becomes independent.

choices.text: Dropping the dimensions
choices.why: Then the shop names are gone.

choices.text: Moving it to a separate database
choices.why: Where it lives does not matter; what it is built from does.

choices.text: Summary tables rebuilt from the star after each load
choices.why: Right. Still built from the star, only rebuilt.

prompt: Match each mart's December figure to its definition.

pairs.right: Books sold in orders not cancelled, by order date
Every payment, shipping included, by order date
Payments by the day they were paid

prompt: What question settles a meeting with three revenue figures?

choices.text: Which team has the most senior analyst?
choices.why: Seniority does not make a definition.

choices.text: Which number did the warehouse produce, so the others can be dropped?
choices.why: Finance's number answers a real question too.

choices.text: Which question does each number answer?
choices.why: Right. Then each can have a name.

choices.text: Which mart was built first?
choices.why: Age is not meaning.

prompt: Finance said 773,739,182 and sales 755,814,482. By how many centavos do they differ?
Why is marketing's December so far below the others?

choices.text: Shop sales have no payment date, so they are all left out
choices.why: Right, and payment dates shift some orders between months as well.

choices.text: Marketing counts only orders that used a promotion code
choices.why: Its SQL has no promotion filter.

choices.text: It subtracts the shipping
choices.why: It includes shipping, like finance.

choices.text: Cancelled orders are counted as negative payments
choices.why: Cancelled orders have no payments in this extract.

prompt: Kimball's answer to three teams with three meanings of one measure: measures, like dimensions, must be ___.
hint: The word lesson 3 used for shared dimensions.

prompt: Which of the differences between the three marts are definitions, rather than defects? Choose all that apply.
hint: A defect is something nobody chose.

choices.text: Including shipping as revenue
choices.why: A choice finance can defend.

choices.text: Dating by payment instead of by order
choices.why: A choice, if written down.

choices.text: Leaving out every sale made in a shop
choices.why: Nobody chose that; it came from the website's habits.

choices.text: Excluding cancelled orders
choices.why: The warehouse's own rule.

prompt: In a bus matrix, what are the rows and the columns?

choices.text: Rows are tables, columns their owners
choices.why: Ownership is the mesh's question.

choices.text: Rows are marts, columns the teams that read each one
choices.why: Readers are not in it.

choices.text: Rows are dimensions, columns their attributes
choices.why: Attributes belong to a dimension's own table.

choices.text: Rows are business processes, columns conformed dimensions
choices.why: Right. An x says the process uses that dimension.

prompt: In the matrix Ana's warehouse generated, how many fact tables carry the customer dimension?
hint: Count the x in one column.

prompt: Why is the shop cell of `fact_fulfilment` empty?

choices.text: The load forgot to join dim_shop
choices.why: It is a decision the matrix makes visible, not a slip.

choices.text: Only the online shop ships, so it would hold one value
choices.why: Right. An empty cell can be a decision.

choices.text: Fulfilment is measured per customer and never per place, by Kimball's rule for accumulating snapshots
choices.why: No such rule; it is about this business.

choices.text: Shops are a type 2 dimension
choices.why: dim_shop is not type 2, and that would not stop a join.

prompt: A team proposes a new mart for author events. What does the bus matrix ask it to do first?

choices.text: Write its row, reusing existing columns
choices.why: Right. New dimensions are built once, for everybody.

choices.text: Build its own customer dimension, so it does not wait for the warehouse team
choices.why: That is how independent marts begin.

choices.text: Copy fact_sales and filter it
choices.why: Events are a different process with a different grain.

choices.text: Choose a format
choices.why: The matrix is about dimensions, not storage.

prompt: Match each data mesh principle to what it means.

pairs.right: The team that runs a process publishes its data
Storage and pipelines provided to every domain

prompt: What problem is data mesh proposed for?

choices.text: Warehouses that cannot store enough data
choices.why: It is about people, not storage.

choices.text: Queries that are slow because the star has too many joins
choices.why: The mesh does not change the model.

choices.text: A central team that every question queues for
choices.why: Right. In a company of many teams, it cannot learn every domain.

choices.text: The cost of cloud warehouses
choices.why: A mesh adds a platform; it does not cut a bill.

prompt: What does a mesh change about the modelling of lessons 2 to 6?

choices.text: Domains publish raw tables, and consumers model them
choices.why: That is the swamp; products are meant to be usable as published.

choices.text: Who does it
choices.why: Right. A domain still declares grains and keeps history.

choices.text: Conformed dimensions are no longer needed, since each domain owns its own
choices.why: Federated governance exists to keep them.

choices.text: Facts and dimensions give way to documents
choices.why: Nothing in the mesh says so.

prompt: Which of these are parts of a data product, as the section describes it? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The code that builds it
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Its metadata
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Written guarantees
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: A dashboard of its own
choices.why: Dashboards are its users.

prompt: What does a product have that a well-named table does not?

choices.text: A faster storage format
choices.why: Format is not the point.

choices.text: A price per query
choices.why: Product is about responsibility, not billing.

choices.text: Its own copy of every dimension, so it never depends on another team
choices.why: That would make it an independent mart.

choices.text: Users who never built it, and use it without asking
choices.why: Right. Everything else follows from that.

prompt: Why does `check_contract.py` exit with status 1 on a breach rather than printing a warning?

choices.text: Python cannot print to standard error from inside a loop over JSON
choices.why: It can; that is not the reason.

choices.text: DuckDB requires it when a table is read-only
choices.why: The status is the program's choice.

choices.text: So a pipeline stops
choices.why: Right. A warning is read when somebody remembers.

choices.text: To undo the rename automatically before anyone sees it
choices.why: It refuses; it does not repair.

prompt: Where should the contract check run?

choices.text: In the producer's pipeline, before publishing
choices.why: Right. The rename is refused where it can be undone.

choices.text: In every consumer's dashboard, before it draws
choices.why: Then every consumer finds it separately, as in lesson 10.

choices.text: Once a month, by the platform team
choices.why: A month of broken dashboards first.

choices.text: Only when a consumer complains
choices.why: That is no contract at all.

prompt: An agreement between a dataset's producer and its consumers, written so a machine can check it, is a data ___.
What does a metadata-driven pipeline buy that matters more than saved typing?

choices.text: No program to maintain, since the metadata runs itself
choices.why: The generator is a program the team maintains.

choices.text: Faster queries on the generated tables
choices.why: The tables are the same as by hand.

choices.text: Type 2 history without writing it
choices.why: The section says that layer is better written.

choices.text: Consistency
choices.why: Right. Every table loads the same way, so one fix fixes all.

prompt: How many staging columns did the generated layer and the hand-written one each have?
Why is the comparison with the hand-written staging layer worth keeping?

choices.text: It shows the generated SQL runs faster than the hand-written SQL
choices.why: It compares columns, not time.

choices.text: It is the generator's test, rerun on every change
choices.why: Right. A generated layer is trusted because it was compared.

choices.text: It finds rows that differ between the two
choices.why: It compares names and types, not rows.

choices.text: DuckDB refuses to run generated SQL that has not been compared
choices.why: DuckDB knows nothing of where SQL came from.

prompt: Which layer is the worst candidate for generating from metadata?

choices.text: The gold layer's business logic
choices.why: Right. A template would be as complex as the program.

choices.text: Staging
choices.why: Fifteen copies of one pattern: the best case.

choices.text: Type 1 dimensions
choices.why: Regular overwrites generate well.

choices.text: Data Vault hubs, links and satellites
choices.why: Their regularity is why vault automation exists.

prompt: What does the lesson recommend for Ponto Final?

choices.text: A data mesh, so each shop owns its sales data
choices.why: A platform with one customer.

choices.text: Keep the three marts and average them
choices.why: An average of three definitions answers no question.

choices.text: A star with marts as views
choices.why: Right, and the independent marts retired once reconciled.

choices.text: A lakehouse in medallion layers, replacing DuckDB with a cluster
choices.why: Nothing in its size calls for that.

prompt: A company of 40 product teams has one central data team with a six-month backlog, and no shared platform. What should come first?

choices.text: Tell every team to build its own marts from now on
choices.why: Without a platform and governance, that is independent marts.

choices.text: A platform and shared rules
choices.why: Right. Domain ownership needs something to stand on.

choices.text: Hire until the central team's backlog is gone
choices.why: The bottleneck is knowledge of 40 domains, not headcount alone.

choices.text: Rewrite the warehouse as a lakehouse
choices.why: Storage format is not the problem described.
